## Today in one sentence {.lecture-opening}

::: {.lecture-summary}
[In this course you learn how computer scientists approach everyday decisions, and how to turn these ideas into Python code.]{.statement}
:::

::: {.lecture-why}
[Why it matters]{.eyebrow}

More and more business decisions rely on data and algorithms. You don't need to become a programmer, but understanding how algorithms think, and writing a few lines of code yourself, makes you a better decision maker. No prior knowledge required.
:::

# [About this course: topics, format and how you pass]{.flow} {.title visibility="hidden"}

## Six topics, one per session

- **I:** Optimal Stopping
- **II:** Explore & Exploit
- **III:** Caching
- **IV:** Scheduling
- **V:** Randomness
- **VI:** Computational Kindness

## Take part, it pays off

- **Participate actively**: it makes the course easier and more fun
- Inspired by the book [Algorithms to Live By]{.highlight}[^3]
- All material is online: [courses.nilsroemer.com](https://courses.nilsroemer.com)

::: {.notes}
Today's agenda in detail: about the course and expectations, how to learn programming (mindset and resources), setting up Python with uv and VS Code, using notebooks with uv, Q&A and next steps.
:::

[^3]: Christian, B., & Griffiths, T. (2016). Algorithms to live by: the computer science of human decisions. First international edition. New York, Henry Holt and Company.

## Each session: lecture, then tutorial

- **Lecture:** we discuss an algorithm for everyday decisions
- **Tutorial:** step-by-step assignments, solved together in groups
- **Difficulty:** depends on your programming experience

. . .

:::{.callout-tip}
No worries, we will help you out if you have any questions!
:::

::: {.notes}
Lecture: presentation and discussion of algorithms related to everyday decision-making. Tutorial: step-by-step assignments to be solved and discussed together in groups. Difficulty: strongly depends on your background and programming experience.
:::

## How you pass

- **Pass/fail course** without exams
- [75% attendance]{.highlight} required
- **Two assignments** on algorithmic problems from the course
- **Short final presentation** of your prototype in the last lecture
- You can work in groups of **up to three students**

## How to hand in assignments

- Each group submits **one solution** per assignment
- Hand in your **working notebooks**
- Due by the **end of the quarter**, earlier is better
- At least **50%** of the solutions have to be correct

::: {.notes}
Earlier submissions are highly encouraged: you get feedback while the topic is still fresh.
:::

## You learn Python in the tutorials

We will mostly **not cover Python during the lectures!**

. . .

[Question:]{.question} Does anybody know why?

. . .

- The best way to learn is by **doing**
- Lectures focus on the decision-making algorithms
- You learn Python by [doing the tutorials]{.highlight}

::: {.notes}
In our experience, the best way to learn programming is by doing. Don't worry, we will help you out if you have any questions.
:::

## Programming is like a new language

- At first it might be [a little bit overwhelming]{.highlight}
- First you get used to it and learn words
- Later you apply it and see results
- Important: *Practice, practice, practice!*

## What you take home

- The [basics of programming]{.highlight}
- **Algorithmic thinking**: how computer scientists approach a problem
- Methods you can **apply** to practical problems

## Why Python?

- **Simple syntax**: easy to read and to learn
- **Versatile**: web, data analysis, artificial intelligence
- **Big community**: help and documentation everywhere

::: {.notes}
Origins: Python was conceived in the late 1980s as a teaching and scripting language. Its syntax is mostly straightforward and very easy to learn. It is used in web development, data analysis, artificial intelligence and more, and it has a large community of users worldwide with extensive documentation.
:::

## Learn first, then use AI

- In the tutorials, [write the code yourself]{.highlight}: that's how you learn
- At the end of the course, you build a small project **with AI support**
- Until then: if you use AI, ask it to **explain**, not to solve

::: {.notes}
AI assistants are powerful, but learning to program means struggling a bit yourself. We use AI deliberately in the final project phase.
:::

# [How to learn programming]{.flow} {.title visibility="hidden"}

## Roadmap {.section-roadmap}

2. [How to learn programming]{.roadmap-item .current}
3. [Setting up Python]{.roadmap-item .future}

## Three habits that work

1. [Be present]{.highlight}: attend the lecture and solve the tutorials
2. [Put in some work]{.highlight}: repeat code and try to understand it
3. [Do coding]{.highlight}: run code, play around, modify, and solve

::: {.notes}
Great resources to start are books (see the list at the end of the lecture) and small challenges, for example on [Codewars](https://www.codewars.com/).
:::

## Don't give up!

- Programming is [problem solving]{.highlight}, errors are normal
- Expect to **stretch** your comfort zone

# [Setting up Python]{.flow} {.title visibility="hidden"}

## Roadmap {.section-roadmap}

1. [About this course: topics, format and how you pass]{.roadmap-item .done}
2. [How to learn programming]{.roadmap-item .done}
3. [Setting up Python]{.roadmap-item .current}
:::

## VS Code is where you write code

- Like **Word for text**, but for code: an app to **write, run and find mistakes** in code
- Apps like this are called [IDEs]{.highlight} (Integrated Development Environments)
- We use VS Code for the **whole course**

::: {.notes}
Other IDEs exist, for example PyCharm or Zed. We use VS Code because it is free, works on all systems and has good notebook support. Every step of the setup is in the Installation Guide on the website, with a check at the end of each step.
:::

## The terminal: typing instead of clicking

- A window where you **type a command**, press Enter, and the computer **answers with text**
- No menus, no buttons: the computer does exactly what you typed
- We need it only for the **setup**: a handful of commands, all in the guide to copy

::: {.notes}
The terminal lives inside VS Code, as a panel at the bottom. On a Mac the line ends with a percent sign, on Windows it starts with PS for PowerShell. Nobody needs to memorise commands: during the setup, you copy them from the guide, paste them and wait until the line is back.
:::

## `uv` installs Python for us

- `uv` is a small **helper tool**: it installs Python and everything Python needs
- Everyone gets the **same Python version**, so code works the same on every laptop
- You install `uv` **once**, then it does the rest for you

::: {.notes}
Without a tool like uv, every laptop ends up with a slightly different Python, and we would spend the tutorials fixing setups instead of programming. uv also keeps each project in its own folder with its own packages, so nothing gets mixed up.
:::

## Notebooks mix text and code

- A notebook is a document with **text cells** and **code cells**
- You run a code cell, and the result appears **right below it**
- All tutorials are notebooks: **read, run, change, try again**

::: {.notes}
Notebooks are ideal for learning: you see a short explanation, run a few lines, and immediately see what happens. VS Code opens them with the Jupyter extension. The tutorials on the website can be downloaded as notebooks under "Other Formats".
:::

## Checkpoint 2: The terminal shows a version number for `uv`

- Your folder `programming-course` is open in VS Code
- A terminal is open at the bottom, and it answers to `uv` with a line like `uv 0.11.26`

. . .

[Guide: Steps 3 to 5](../general/uv.qmd#step-3-create-your-course-folder){.guide-ref}

Most common problem here: uv is "not found". Almost always, VS Code was not closed and reopened after the installation.

## Checkpoint 3: You see Hello from programming-course!

- Python 3.13 is installed
